input: A single-stage machine compressing nitrogen offers a compact illustration of the same temperature story told by every isentropic estimate. The compressor raises nitrogen from 1 bar to 4 bar, and the gas enters at an inlet temperature of 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 435 K. That discharge figure, like every isentropic figure, is an idealisation: the estimate deliberately leaves mechanical losses out of account, and the moving parts of a real machine return those losses to the gas as heat. It is therefore no surprise that the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate. The estimate marks the floor that the compression alone would set, and the installed machine runs above that floor by exactly the amount its own imperfections contribute, which is why the two numbers belong together in any honest account of the machine. That is the real function of such an estimate in practice. It separates, cleanly and in advance, the temperature the gas must reach simply by being compressed from the further temperature the machinery of a particular installation adds on top, and it does so before a single measurement on the installed unit is taken. Discussions of condition, of fouling, of wear, and of performance all become sharper once that separation has been made, because each of them can then be attached to the gap where it belongs instead of being spread loosely over the whole discharge figure.
target: Nitrogen is compressed in a single stage from 1 bar to 4 bar, and the isentropic discharge temperature is calculated from the inlet state. The inlet temperature is 293 K and the heat-capacity ratio is 1.4. The estimate gives a discharge temperature of 435 K. The temperature rise follows the pressure rise in the compression; the estimate holds the compression isentropic, and no property of the machine enters it. The limit of the result is stated with it: mechanical losses are excluded from the isentropic estimate, and the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher. A measured temperature equal to the estimate would leave the losses unaccounted for. The result is valid for the stated inlet temperature, pressures, and heat-capacity ratio, and it is the baseline against which the installed machine's discharge temperature is read. The calculation is a statement about the gas, not about the machine. Nothing in it depends on the size of the compressor, the speed at which it runs, or the condition of its parts; those enter only through the losses the estimate excludes. The discharge temperature is therefore the reference temperature for the stated rise in pressure. Plant readings are compared with it in that spirit: the measured temperature is the temperature of a real compression, and the estimate is the temperature of the same compression with the machine taken out of the account. The gap between them belongs to the machine, and it is reported with the measured temperature wherever the comparison is used.
